extracted.intended_audience: researchers and practitioners in federated learning, machine learning security, and privacy engineering
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines, open problems, and evaluation criteria for designing, attacking, and defending federated learning systems with respect to privacy, robustness, and user perception. Covers adversary models, attack vectors, defenses, and user-facing considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve privacy by considering both what and how
rubrics_metrics.description: Preserving the privacy of user data requires considering both what function of the data is being computed and how the computation is executed (and in particular, who can see/influence intermediate results).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Techniques for the “what” include data minimization and differential privacy; techniques for the “how” include MPC, homomorphic encryption, and trusted execution environments. Open challenges include adapting DP accounting to real-world deployments, multi-actor/multi-model training, time-evolving data, client availability, and maintaining utility without rapidly depleting privacy budgets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use data minimization and differential privacy for the 'what'
rubrics_metrics.description: Techniques for addressing the “what” include data minimization and differential privacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It remains an open challenge how best to adapt differential privacy accounting and privatization techniques to real world deployments including numerous models over overlapping populations, time-evolving data, and non-determinancies such as client availability while maintaining high utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use secure computation/TEEs for the 'how'
rubrics_metrics.description: Techniques for addressing the “how” include secure multi-party computation (MPC), homomorphic encryption (HE), and trusted execution environments (TEEs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MPC techniques have been deployed at scale for some functionalities, but many functionalities are still far more communication- and computation-expensive than insecure counterparts. Producing reliably exploit-immune TEE platforms and connecting attested binaries to privacy properties remains immature; these are important practical constraints when selecting defenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compose techniques for Privacy in Depth
rubrics_metrics.description: Techniques should be composed to enable Privacy in Depth, with privacy expectations degrading gracefully even if one technique/component of the system is compromised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design systems so that compromises in one component do not catastrophically break privacy; composition and graceful degradation are design desiderata.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer distributed differential privacy under appropriate trust models
rubrics_metrics.description: Distributed differential privacy best combines what and how techniques to offer high accuracy and high privacy under an honest-but-curious server, a trusted third-party, or a trusted execution environment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select DP instantiations based on the assumed trust model; distributed DP may perform best when some trusted component exists, but trust assumptions must be explicit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enable verifiability of execution
rubrics_metrics.description: Verifiability enables parties to prove that they have executed their parts of a computation faithfully.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Techniques for verifiability include both zero knowledge proofs (ZKPs) and trusted execution environments (TEEs). Verifiability is important for detecting malicious aggregators or dishonest participants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for adversarial server threats
rubrics_metrics.description: Strong protection against an adversarial server remains a significant open problem for federation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design and evaluate defenses under adversarial server threat models; some defenses (e.g., ZKPs, MPC) can help but are expensive and/or limited in scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Private sub-model training and user choice privacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Achieve communication-efficient sub-model federated learning while keeping the client’s sub-model choice private.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Promising approaches include private information retrieval (PIR) for private sub-model download and sparse secure aggregation for updates. Open problems: characterize sparsity regimes of practical interest, develop sparse secure aggregation that is communication-efficient in those regimes, and co-optimize PIR and secure aggregation to share costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain sparsity under distributed differential privacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Distributed DP often adds noise to all vector elements, turning sparse updates into dense privatized updates with high probability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open question: whether there exists an instantiation of distributed differential privacy that maintains sparsity of model updates; resolving this tension is important for sub-model training.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communicate protections and limits to users clearly
rubrics_metrics.description: Make the benefits and limitations of a specific FL implementation intuitive to the average user; be clear about what protections it does (and does not) provide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design user-facing explanations of FL and exactly what data will be sent. Consider whether FL might give users a false sense of privacy and how to enable users to feel safe and actually be safe as they learn more.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elicit and incorporate user privacy preferences
rubrics_metrics.description: Allow users to specify what inferences they allow and disallow, and incorporate those preferences into the FL model.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preferences could be enforced on-device (filtering updates) or during aggregation. Need technical tools for preference elicitation and methods to incorporate preferences into training; Pufferfish framework is one formalism to specify protected predicates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behavioral research for preference elicitation and education
rubrics_metrics.description: Any approach requiring users to specify privacy standards should include behavioral or field research with an educational component and preference measurement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Educational component should measure and improve user understanding of privacy technology and data use. Preference elicitation should occur in labs, field experiments, or focus groups with informed, representative participants; studies must be ethical and avoid deception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify adversary goals: untargeted vs targeted
rubrics_metrics.description: Adversarial goals generally fall into untargeted attacks (model downgrade/global accuracy reduction) and targeted attacks (backdoors affecting a minority of examples while preserving overall accuracy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize continuum between goals; defenses and measurements should consider both extremes and intermediate goals (e.g., degrading accuracy except on small subsets).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specify adversary capabilities along key axes
rubrics_metrics.description: Adversary capabilities should be clearly defined across axes: attack vector, model inspection (black/stale-white/white-box), participant collusion (non-colluding, cross-update, within-update), participation rate, and adaptability (static/dynamic).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these axes (Table 11) to evaluate applicability and strength of attacks and defenses; federated settings change these axes relative to datacenter training (e.g., model broadcast often implies white-box access).

rubrics_metrics.name: Model attack vectors distinctly: data poisoning, model update poisoning, evasion
rubrics_metrics.description: Different attack vectors: data poisoning (alter client datasets), model update poisoning (alter reports/updates sent to server), and evasion (manipulate inference-time inputs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each vector has different constraints and defenses; model update poisoning is often strictly more powerful in federated settings because adversaries can craft arbitrary updates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat Byzantine threat model for untargeted attacks
rubrics_metrics.description: For untargeted model update poisoning, consider the Byzantine threat model where faulty/adversarial nodes can produce arbitrary outputs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Byzantine attacks are worst-case untargeted attacks; defenses should consider Byzantine-resilient aggregation mechanisms but be aware theoretical guarantees rely on assumptions that may not hold (non-IID data, unreliable clients).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use robust aggregation but validate applicability
rubrics_metrics.description: Byzantine-resilient defenses replace averaging with robust mean estimators (median-based, Krum, trimmed mean) to tolerate arbitrary/malicious updates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although provably effective under assumptions, empirical results in federated settings are mixed; evaluate robustness empirically for non-IID data, limited participation, and adaptive adversaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider redundancy and data shuffling tradeoffs
rubrics_metrics.description: Redundancy and data shuffling can mitigate Byzantine attacks but generally assume server access to or ability to globally shuffle data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These approaches increase communication costs and may be incompatible with FL goals of minimizing communication and preserving client data locality; reconciling these tradeoffs is an open problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipate stealthy targeted/backdoor attacks and their detection limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Targeted model update poisoning (backdoors) can be stealthy and introduced with few adversaries, often appearing similar to benign updates and evading anomaly detectors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Existing defenses often require access to training data or clean holdout sets. Potential avenues: zero-knowledge proofs to show updates have pre-specified properties, hardware attestation, or other methods that do not require raw data access.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defend against collusion and sybil attacks without data inspection
rubrics_metrics.description: Colluding adversaries or many sybil clients can make attacks more effective and harder to detect in federated learning, since the server cannot inspect client data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop defenses that detect or mitigate collusion and sybil strategies without access to client data; this remains challenging and important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data sanitization and pruning require clean holdout data
rubrics_metrics.description: Data sanitization (remove poisoned/anomalous data) and network pruning (remove neurons inactive on clean data) are defenses against data poisoning/backdoors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These defenses often require access to representative clean data or a holdout set, which may not be available in FL without privacy loss; determining federated-compatible versions of these defenses is an open question.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantify relation between data poisoning and model update poisoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Data poisoning is a special case of model update poisoning, but the gap between their achievable effects is unclear and likely depends on corrupted client counts and model overparameterization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical and theoretical work (e.g., using machine teaching perspectives) is needed to quantify when and by how much model update poisoning is stronger than data poisoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for inference-time evasion (adversarial examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evasion attacks manipulate deployed model inputs to cause misclassification; adversarial examples can be white-box or black-box.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federated learning increases white-box exposure because models are broadcast; defenses should address white-box attacks. Evaluate robustness across types of perturbations and threat models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use adversarial training but recognize limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Adversarial training (training with adversarial examples via minimax optimization) generally provides some robustness to white-box evasion attacks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is no canonical adversarial training formulation; hyperparameters and optimization choices significantly affect robustness. Adversarial training often only protects against the specific types of adversarial examples used in training and may not generalize to other attacks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not rely solely on accuracy metrics to detect backdoors
rubrics_metrics.description: Global training accuracy or per-client accuracy may not detect the presence of backdoors, since backdoored models can maintain high overall accuracy while misbehaving on small targeted subsets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop detection metrics and monitoring procedures that can reveal targeted misbehavior (e.g., triggered-only inputs) without violating client privacy.
